cipal route of gaseous exchange. (A) Leaf — (B) Woody stem/bark — (C) Root — with
(i) lenticels, (ii) root surface / soil air, (iii) stomata.
Reasoning. Leaves exchange gases through stomata →A–iii. Older stems are sealed
by corky bark, so they rely on lens-shaped lenticels →B–i. Roots exchange directly
with air trapped between soil particles →C–ii. Answer: A–iii, B–i, C–ii. The dis-
tractor here is pairing the woody stem with stomata — but a thick bark has lost most
functional stomata, which is precisely why lenticels exist.
4

The photosynthesis–respiration overlap (a classic trap). In a green leaf during
the day, two opposite gas exchanges run at once: respiration consumes O2 and re-
leases CO2, while photosynthesis consumes CO2 and releases O2. Because daytime
photosynthesis usually runs faster, the leaf shows a net uptake of CO2 and net release
of O2 — and crucially, the O2 produced inside the cell by photosynthesis largely satis-
fies that same cell’s respiratory need, so little external O2 is even required. At night,
with photosynthesis switched off, the picture is simple: only respiration operates, so
the plant takes in O2 and gives out CO2, just like any other organism. Students who
claim “plants release O2 and take in CO2” have described only daytime photosynthesis
and forgotten that respiration never st

Section 8: Cheat Sheet
• Plants have NO respiratory organs and need none — gas exchange is by
diffusion, cell by cell.
• Four reasons: each part self-sufficient ⋅short diffusion distances ⋅continuous
intercellular air spaces ⋅low O2 demand (much tissue is dead/inactive).
• Routes: leaves →stomata; woody stems/old roots →lenticels; roots →soil
air / root surface.
• Day vs night: daytime leaf nets CO2 in / O2 out (photosynthesis > respiration);
night = O2 in / CO2 out (respiration only).
• Aerenchyma keeps waterlogged (hydrophyte) roots supplied with O2 from the
shoot.
• Respiration ≠combustion:
controlled, stepwise, enzyme-driven oxidation
trapping energy in ATP — not an uncontrolled burn.
Memory aids: - “Low demand, short distance” — the whole reason plants skip lungs.
- “Stomata–Lenticel–

Section 2: Key Definitions & Concepts
Respiration: the enzyme-controlled breakdown of food (chiefly glucose) to release
stored chemical energy as ATP. Cellular respiration is this process at the level of the
individual cell.
Breathing / gaseous exchange: the physical exchange of O2 (taken in) and CO2
(given out) between an organism and its environment. In plants this happens by dif-
fusion, cell by cell — there is no bulk “breathing” movement.
Respiratory organ: a specialised structure for gas exchange (lung, gill, trachea).
Plants possess none.
Routes of gaseous exchange in plants: - Stomata — microscopic pores, mainly on
leaf surfaces and young green stems, bounded by guard cells; the principal ga

Section 6: Crack the MCQ
Q1. Plants do not possess specialised respiratory organs mainly because: (a) plants
do not respire at all (b) each plant part meets its own gas-exchange needs over short
diffusion distances (c) plants store oxygen in vacuoles for later use (d) the bloodstream
of plants distributes oxygen efficiently
Correct: (b). Local, short-range diffusion to each part removes the need for organs.
(a) is false — plants respire continuously. (c) is invented; vacuoles do not stockpile O2.
(d) is the classic animal-physiology import — plants have no bloodstream.
Q2. Lenticels are most directly associated with gaseous exchange in: (a) young leaves
(b) guard cells (c) woody stems and old roots (d) root hairs
Correct: (c). Lenticels are pores in bark/periderm that ventilate woody parts

Homology vs Analogy — the highest-yield comparison in the chapter:

Basic structure & embr

• Homology is the cleanest case. A whale’s flipper, a bat’s wing, and a horse’s
leg do utterly different jobs — swimming, flying, running — yet share the same
underlying bones in the same arrangement (humerus, radius–ulna, carpals, pha-
langes). If each had been “designed from scratch” for its function, there would
be no reason to reuse one blueprint. The shared blueprint only makes sense if
all three inherited it from one common ancestor and then diverged. That is
divergent evolution.
• Analogy is the deliberate contrast. An insect’s wing and a bird’s wing both fly,
but are built on entirely different structures. Here the similarity is driven by
the environment (the demands of flight), not by shared ancestry — convergent
evolution. This is why analogy must never be used as evidence of rel

— the sequence of chemical evolution, the Miller–Urey experiment, and
the homology-vs-analogy trap are perennial favourites.
CUET leans on
definitions and scientist–contribution matching. CBSE Boards typically ask
a 2–3 mark “distinguish homologous from analogous organs” or “describe
Miller’s experiment” question. The evidences section is also a goldmine for

Exam Relevance: This is the highest-yield slice of the whole chapter. NEET

role of Ca2+/troponin, and “which band stays constant” are perennial. CBSE
Boards set a 3–5 mark “explain sliding filament theory with the role of Ca2+”

Section 1 — Concept Intuition
In Sub-01 you built the machine — the sarcomere, the thick (myosin) and thin (actin)
filaments, the troponin–tropomyosin guard rail. Now we switch it on. The single most
important idea, and the one students most often get wrong, is this: muscle shortens
without its filaments

Section 2 — Key Definitions & Diagnostic Features
• Sliding filament theory — contraction occurs because thin (actin) filaments slide
over stationary-length thick (myosin) filaments, increasing their overlap and short-
ening the sarcomere.
• Cross-bridge — the temporary attachment formed when an energised myosin
head binds an exposed active site on actin; one myosin filament is surrounded by
about six actin filaments.
• Motor unit — a single motor neuron together with all the muscle fibres it inner-
vates (finer control ⇒fewer fibres per unit).
• Motor end plate / neuromuscular junction (NMJ) — the junction where the
motor neuron’s axon terminal meets the sarcolemma; here the neurotransmitter
(acetylcholine) is released.
• Regulatory vs contractile proteins — contractile: actin + myosin; r

fibre pull “harder”; it grades the strength of a movement by recruiting more motor
units and by firing them more rapidly, so individual twitches fuse (summation) into
a smooth, sustained contraction. This is why you can pick up both a feather and a full
bucket with the same biceps. Cardiac muscle, by contrast, behaves as a single functional
unit — its intercalated discs spread each signal across the whole sheet, so the heart
contracts in an all-or-none fashion as one.
